#### 4.5.1.1.2 Training transcript

A training transcript is the complete record of the training of a machine learning system, including training data, hyperparameters, and a record of the digital objects that constitute the emerging model and attest to its provenance. This includes model weights and weight shards, as well as potentially gradients or activations depending on the training technique.319

#### 4.5.1.1.3 Proof of training

Building on the concepts developed by Shavit (2023), we define a "proof of training" as ev- idence that is sufficient to prove that a given model was generated using a given training transcript.320 Provided with such a proof, the Verifier would then have extremely strong evidence that the model was indeed trained in the declared manner.321

#### 4.5.1.2 Potential political goals

##### 4.5.1.2.1 Inhibit or ban development of extremely large models

States may make an agreement which verifiably inhibits their ability to produce mod- els above a certain size-measured via quantities such as compute budget or parameter

\* 318 Shavit 2023 and Choi, Shavid, and Duvenaud 2023 both grapple with this problem. As they note, in theory, it should be possible for the Prover and Verifier to create highly reproducible training techniques, although this may not currently be possible with leading edge AI training hardware. Whether or not highly reproducible training remains a serious technical difficulty-or source of significant training inefficiency-moving forward is a question that deserves urgent work.

\* 319 Shavit.

\* 320 Dami Choi, Yonadav Shavit, and David Duvenaud, 'Tools for Verifying Neural Models' Training Data' (arXiv, 2 July 2023), https ://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2307.00682; Shavit, 'What Does It Take to Catch a Chinchilla?'

\* 321 Given enough data and compute, it is possible to replicate parts of the training run exactly, thus allowing for targeted or even very extensive examination of the training results. In the limit, this would be as computationally costly as building the model in the first place. Faster alternatives to such a process would therefore be desirable. See Shavit, 'What Does It Take to Catch a Chinchilla?' and 'AICert', Mithril Security, accessed 2 October 2024, https://www.mithrilsecurity.io/aicert.

<!-- PageFooter: page 104 -->
<!-- PageBreak -->

count.322,323 This policy goal is premised on the widespread acknowledgement that ex- tremely large models are particularly likely to generate novel capabilities and risks.324 De- pending on the political goals, a continuum of potential agreements are available, ranging from blunt inhibition mechanisms up to fine-grained controls. Blunt mechanisms involve making broad changes to either compute chips or how they are physically arranged to make it more costly and slow to produce large models. By contrast, fine-grained controls are spe- cific mechanisms that could prevent the production of extremely large models in a variety of ways, while having less of an effect on other uses of compute. The efficiency of most AI development would be better served by fine-grained rather than blunt mechanisms. More- over, a true ban is likely impossible via blunt mechanisms, but is potentially workable via fine-grained controls.

query_text: In the responsible-AI standards chapter on Explicability, who must make an AI system's final decision, and what should users be able to do when they think it erred?
reference_answer: A human should always make the final decision, since systems should never be fully autonomous. Users must also have a built-in way to report a mistake when they think the prediction or decision is wrong.
generated_output: In the responsible-AI standards chapter on Explicability, it is stated that a human should always make the final decision regarding an AI system. Additionally, users must be able to express their concerns if they believe the system has made a mistake in its prediction or decision. This should be included in the design of the solution to increase user trust.

context_data.content:
# 4- Explicability

As described in introduction, AI is a system, with users to take into account and an interface to build. Once you have access to what factor influenced your prediction/decision, it comes the time to explain it to your users. That is what explicability is. Knowing your users, understanding not only their needs but their reluctances, choosing the right level of information, giving them control and ability to give feedbacks, all of these techniques will ensure more trust and adoption of your solution.

# A. UX studies

You need to know the appetite of users relative to AI to deliver the right level of explicability.

With explicability, we enter into UX Design and question the preference of users in terms of presentation of results. The level of explicability that accompanies the decision must correspond to the profile of the users. Depending on how AI will impact their work and life, but also on their maturity vis-à-vis this technology, not everyone will need the same granularity in the explanation.

To know the appetite of your users for AI, the best thing is to ask them the question through a short questionnaire. This will make it possible to detect the populations towards which it will be necessary to make a special effort to achieve genuine support.

Moreover, you won't give the same information to an expert or a novice. For example, for a medical diagnostic algorithm, you won't give the same information to doctors or patients. Doctors will need more technical information, patients more plain English ones. Workshops with your users and regular feedbacks are indispensable to fit your interface with their information requirements to trust your solution.

## 09 APPENDICES

### APPENDIX 1: GLOSSARY

· Accountability: Accountability can be broken down into two subcomponents: answerability and auditability. Answerability refers to establishing a continuous chain of human responsibility across the whole AI project delivery workflow and demands that explanations and justifications of both the content of algorithmically supported decisions and the processes behind their production be offered by competent human authorities in plain, understandable, and coherent language. Auditability answers the question of how the designers and implementers of AI systems are to be held accountable. This aspect of accountability has to do with demonstrating both the responsibility of design and use practices and the justifiability of outcomes.

· Algorithm: An algorithm is a procedure or series of steps that provide instructions on how to take a series of inputs and produce an output. For instance, a recipe can be thought of as an algorithm that provides instructions for taking a series of inputs (i.e. the ingredients) and creating an output (e.g. a cake). In the case of machine learning, the algorithm is typically a series of instructions that instruct a software package to take a dataset (i.e. the input) and learn a model or discover some underlying pattern (i.e. the output).

· Algorithmic Audits: There are a variety of approaches to algorithmic auditing, which range from the targeted assessment of a system according to some metric (e.g. level of bias) to a broader approach that focuses on whether the system complies with a set of norms or regulatory area. While typically performed by professionals for the purpose of independent assessment, algorithmic audits have also been used by journalists, academics, and activists as a means of securing greater levels of transparency and accountability.

· Automated decision: An automated decision is the selection of an action or a recommendation made using computational processes. Automated decisions describe those that either augment or replace decisional work typically performed by humans alone. Most commonly, automated decisions are predictions about persons or conditions in the world derived from machine learning analysis of data about past events and its similarity to a given set of conditions.

· Automated decision system: An automated decision system (ADS) augments or replaces human decision-making by using computational processes to produce answers to questions either as discrete classifications (e.g. yes, no; male, female, non-binary; malignant, benign) or continuous scores (e.g. degree of creditworthiness, risk of crime occurrence, projected tumour growth). Most ADS produce predictions about persons or conditions using machine learning and other computational logic by calculating the probability that a given condition is met.

### 2) Right to explanation of individual decision-making (Article 86)

Article 86 provides that any legal or natural persons are entitled to an explanation when a decision is made using an AI tool. This right to explanation applies when the decision is taken on the basis of the output of a high-risk AI system, and it has legal consequences or significantly affects the person in a manner they deem detrimental to their health, safety, or fundamental rights. The explanation provided must be clear and meaningful and provide the necessary information "on the role of the Al system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken." However, this provision applies solely to high-risk AI systems.

The specific benefits of this provision in relation to existing laws remain unclear, particularly because Article 22 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) already guarantees a right to an explanation for decisions made automatically. Nonetheless, this provision appears to extend the right to an explanation to include scenarios where a human decides "on the basis of the output" from an Al system, not just decisions "based solely on automated processing," as stipulated by Article 22 of the GDPR.

## 1.16. Probability calibration

# C. Confidence intervals

Another interesting information to provide to the users: the confidence interval. This allows you to know on which subcategories of data the model is reliable, and for which, not so much. It is directly related to the variability in the prediction for a certain range of predictions and very much depends on how much data of each subcategories the model has been trained. For example, if a model has been trained with a lot of Caucasian faces and a few Asian ones, it will tend to be more reliable for the first class.

<!-- PageBreak -->

## C.1. Cross validation

You can get a first measure of the variability of your overall model performance by doing cross-validation (3.1. Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance ), but it is not enough as it doesn't go into the details of performance for the subcategories.

## C.2. Mapie

You can use a toolbox called Mapie (MAPIE - Model Agnostic Prediction Interval Estimator - MAPIE 0.6.5 documentation ) which is a model agnostic solution that works for both regression and classification problems.

Source : Taquet et al. 2022 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12274.pdf

You can find a video explaining the solution here : https://crossminds.ai/video/mapie- model-agnostic-prediction-interval-estimator-614bc17e3c7a224a9090211b/

And articles here:

· With MAPIE, uncertainties are back in machine learning !

· https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12274.pdf

# D. Human agency/control

In a Pew Research report from 2018 on AI and the Future of Humans (Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Humans ) concern about Human agency came out as the main concern. They talk about the fear that : 'the use of Al reduces individuals' control over their lives'.

And the European Commission High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence (AI HLEG 2018 : Requirements of Trustworthy Al ) defines 'human agency and oversight' as the first of seven key elements in their "Trustworthy Al" framework. They state that 'Al systems should support human autonomy and decision-making, as prescribed by the principle of respect for human autonomy. This requires that AI systems should both act as enablers to a democratic, flourishing and equitable society by supporting the user's agency and foster fundamental rights, and allow for human oversight."

Following these reports, it is fundamental that your systems always keep the 'humans in the loop' and should never be fully autonomous. A human should always make the final decision.

<!-- PageBreak -->

This recommendation goes hand-in-hand with explicability as you should give all the necessary information to the users to make the decision.

And the design of the interface of the product or solution you are developing will be key here.

# E. Feedback loops

Because keeping people in the loop is fundamental as we have just seen, care will be taken to encourage user feedback on the solution.

## E.1. Report a mistake

If your user considers that the system has made a mistake in the prediction or decision, they must be able to express it. You should include, in the design of your solution, a way for them to do so.

This will increase the trust of your users for your solution greatly.

## E.2. Performance in production

In addition, this feedback can be used to measure the performance in production, detect drifts and give a database to eventually retrain your model.

Moreover, you can also detect bugs in the system and be able to strengthen its robustness and performance.

And here is an interesting article on the feedback loop topic: Feedback Loops-Friend or Foe?

<!-- PageBreak -->

## Article 86 Right to explanation of individual decision-making

1. Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer on the basis of the output from a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, with the exception of systems listed under point 2 thereof, and which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects that person in a way that they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety or fundamental rights shall have the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken.

2. Paragraph 1 shall not apply to the use of AI systems for which exceptions from, or restrictions to, the obligation under that paragraph follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law.

· To establish subject fairness, we can ask if the person who is subject to a decision or action taken by or supported by an AI system perceives the process and outcome as justifiable and legitimate. To establish justifiability and legitimacy, the subject may need to know the details of how the decision or action was arrived at and what factors might have led to another outcome (e.g. a recruiting algorithm rejects a job applicant, which can be explained by showing that the applicant lacks a specifically named skill or credential). A subject also needs access to recourse if they disagree with the outcome (e.g. a job applicant has the opportunity to offer additional information or question the accuracy of the recruiting algorithm to a human with authority to alter the outcome).

· Implementer fairness can be expressed through accountability measures including processes of auditing and evaluation. Implementers are tasked with ensuring that AI systems are transparent and interpretable by those who use them and who are affected by that use. Prior to and during the use of AI, implementers should take social, economic, and political effects into account, being mindful not only of the perceived benefits of AI but also for the occurrence and risk of harm and who bears it. For example, the introduction of a criminal sentencing algorithm may produce more judicial consistency and/or streamline decision making. However, the same system may also reproduce discriminatory outcomes, such as where people of colour have received longer sentences for similar convictions as whites in white-majority countries, due to some feature of its design or the data it references. Where such conflicts occur, the functional accuracy or efficiency (if present) of an AI should be set aside and the algorithm design and data model should be thoroughly evaluated, including the decision as to whether to use it.

### 02

#### L'IA responsable

#### L'IA RESPONSABLE

Impact AI propose une définition et un choix de méthodes de mise en œuvre d'une IA responsable. Le collectif répertorie des outils conformes à des valeurs éthiques, les met à disposition de tous et vérifie leur pertinence dans le temps.

##### Qu'est-ce que l'IA responsable ?

C'est une intelligence artificielle conçue pour rester toujours sous le contrôle humain. Elle est fiable et robuste c'est-à-dire qu'elle fait ce qu'elle promet et que son fonctionnement garantit sûreté et sécurité. Elle est aussi respectueuse du droit, du consentement de l'utilisateur, de la vie privée et des libertés fondamentales ; son fonctionnement est explicable et transparent. Au-delà de la responsabilité des utilisateurs de l'IA, cette définition questionne celles des développeurs et des organisations. La conviction d'Impact Al est qu'il faut passer d'un usage responsable à une IA responsable par essence, by design. Au-delà des objectifs louables poursuivis par les services développés, l'intelligence artificielle doit comporter la notion de responsabilité dans son ADN.

\* 1288 Recital 22 states that the safety that the public at large is entitled to expect "should be assessed by taking into account, inter alia, the intended purpose, reasonably foreseeable use, the presentation, the objective characteristics and the properties of the product in question, including its expected lifespan, as well as the specific requirements of the group of users for whom the product is intended."

<!-- PageFooter: Table of Contents Chapter 5 Contents page 248 -->
<!-- PageBreak -->

<!-- PageHeader: CHAPTER 5 Regulatory initiatives REGULATING UNDER UNCERTAINTY: Governance Options for Generative AI -->

Interestingly, the revised PLD provides in Recital 30 that "the assessment of defectiveness should involve an objective analysis of the safety that the public at large is entitled to expect, and not refer to the safety that any particular person is entitled to expect". However, does the public have sufficient awareness of the recognized risk of hallucinations inherent in models like ChatGPT, especially when it has been explicitly stated that these models can make errors? Recital 31 specifies that "warnings or other information provided with a product cannot be considered sufficient to make an otherwise defective product safe, since defectiveness should be determined by reference to the safety that the public at large is entitled to expect." Thus, one could conclude that merely warning users that a model might hallucinate, produce inaccurate information, or behave unpredictably does not suffice to exempt that product from being deemed defective. On the other hand, would it be reasonable to consider that the public expects that such models never produce inaccurate or illegal content? For the moment, there do not seem to be any clear, definitive answers to these questions.

Moreover, it is worth mentioning that "the reasonably foreseeable use of the product"1289 should be considered in the assessment. Does this suggest that the providers of generative AI chatbots should foresee that students, journalists, or lawyers will use their tool and rely on the information it generates? While the answer to that question is uncertain, it is evident that providers of AI systems must foresee potential misuse. Recital 31 provides that the determination "of reasonably foreseeable use should also encompass misuse that is not unreasonable under the circumstances, such as the foreseeable behaviour of a user of machinery resulting from a lack of concentration or the foreseeable behaviour

of certain user groups such as children." Consequently, providers should expect that schoolchildren might use their tools for doing their homework or that teenagers might seek to create deepfakes.

The revised Product Liability Directive also mentions "the effect on the product of its ability to continue to learn or acquire new features after it is placed on the market or put into service."1290 An Al system could be deemed defective due to knowledge acquired after its release. Recital 32 states that "a manufacturer that designs a product with the ability to develop unexpected behaviour should remain liable for behaviour that causes harm."

Once again, it is challenging to ascertain the full impact of such a provision at this stage. The text appears to hold developers of advanced AI models liable for the most unpredictable effects of their applications. In a context where it is inherently impossible to fully anticipate the behavior of machine-learning tools, this responsibility could be substantial.

### d) Possible claimants and repairable damage

While the proposal substantially raises the number of potential defendants, it is relatively narrow in defining who can sue and what kind of compensation they can pursue. Only natural persons are entitled to compensation.1291 This implies that legal entities, beginning with businesses, are not entitled to initiate legal proceedings based on product liability against a provider of an AI system.

The revised PLD extends the scope of recoverable damages to cover death, physical injury, or property damage (unless the property is used for professional

## KEY OBLIGATIONS

-Member States must ensure that effective remedies are available under respective national jurisdictions, including for civil and criminal responsibility, and that accessible redress mechanisms are put in place for individuals whose rights are negatively impacted by the development or use of AI applications.

-Member States should establish public oversight mechanisms for AI systems that may breach legal norms in the sphere of human rights, democracy, or the rule of law.

-Member States should ensure that developers and deployers of AI systems (1) identify, document, and report on potential negative impacts of AI systems on human rights, democracy, and the rule of law; and (2) put in place adequate mitigation measures to ensure responsibility and accountability for any harm caused.

-Member States should put in place measures to ensure that public authorities are always able to audit AI systems used by private actors, so as to assess their compliance with existing legislation and to hold private actors accountable.

-Member States should take adequate measures to counter the use or misuse of AI systems for unlawful interference in electoral processes, for personalised political targeting without adequate transparency, responsibility, and accountability mechanisms, or more generally for shaping voters' political behaviours or to manipulate public opinion.

-Member States should adopt strategies and put in place measures for fighting disinformation and identifying online hate speech to ensure fair informational plurality.

-Member States should subject their public procurement processes to legally binding requirements that ensure the responsible use of AI in the public sector by safeguarding compliance with the above-mentioned principles, including transparency, fairness, responsibility, and accountability.

-Member States should put in place measures to increase digital literacy and skills in all segments of the population. Their educational curricula should adjust to promote a culture of responsible innovations that respects human rights, democracy, and the rule of law.

<!-- PageFooter: page 22 -->
<!-- PageBreak -->

## SUBSTANTIVE RIGHTS

-The right to a fair trial and due process (Art. 6 ECHR). This should also include the possibility of receiving insight into and challenging AI- informed decisions in the context of law enforcement or justice, including the right to review of such decision by a human.

-The right to judicial independence and impartiality, and the right to legal assistance.

-The right to an effective remedy (Art. 13 ECHR), also in case of unlawful harm or breach an individual's human rights in the context of AI systems.

RULE OF LAW

## KEY OBLIGATIONS

-Member States must ensure that AI systems used in the field of justice and law enforcement are in line with the essential requirements of the right to a fair trial. To this end, they should ensure the quality and security of judicial decisions and data, as well as the transparency, impartiality, and fairness of data processing methods. Safeguards for the accessibility and explainability of data processing methods, including the possibility of external audits, should be introduced to this end.

-Member States must ensure that effective remedies are available and that accessible redress mechanisms are put in place for individuals whose rights are violated through the development or use of AI systems in contexts relevant to the rule of law.

-Member States should provide meaningful information to individuals on the use of AI systems in the public sector whenever this can significantly impact individuals' lives. Such information must especially be provided when AI systems are used in the field of justice and law enforcement, both as concerns the role of AI systems within the process, and the right to challenge the decisions informed or made thereby.

-Member States should ensure that use of AI systems does not interfere with the decision- making power of judges or judicial independence and that any judicial decision is subject to meaningful human oversight.

<!-- PageFooter: page 23 -->
<!-- PageBreak -->

## ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR PRINCIPLES, RIGHTS, AND OBLIGATIONS

There are some additional factors that should be weighed when the potential introduction of new rights and obligations in a future principles-based legal framework on AI systems is being considered. First, these rights and obligations should be necessary, useful, and proportionate to the goal of protecting citizens from the negative impacts of AI systems on human rights, democracy, and the rule of law, while at the same time ensuring the just and equitable distribution of their benefits. These considerations of risks and benefits should be comprehensive and should incorporate an awareness of the balance of legitimate interests at stake. A risk-based and benefits-aware approach should also differentiate between different levels of risk and take this into account when regulatory measures are formulated and agreed.

#### DATA PROTECTION AND THE RIGHT TO PRIVACY

The design and use of AI systems that rely on the processing of personal data must secure a person's right to respect for private and family life, including the individual's right to control their own data. Informed, freely given, and unambiguous consent must play a role in this.

##### ACCOUNTABILITY AND RESPONSIBILITY

All persons involved in the design and deployment of AI systems must be held accountable when applicable legal norms are violated or any unjust harm occurs to end-users or to others. Those who are negatively impacted must have access to effective remedy to redress harms.

# B. Probabilities

By highlighting the relevant information, giving the user as much context as possible, it becomes possible to erase the feeling of no longer having any control over the decisions made by the machine.

The first information that will interest the user is to know how reliable the AI recommendation is. We too often set a default decision (i.e. threshold of 50% for a binary decision), and only give users the final decision: yes or no. Knowing the probability of a prediction can be a key acceptability factor. Indeed, depending on

<!-- PageBreak -->

whether this percentage is 60% or 90% for a binary classification, the confidence in your model's predictions will not be the same.

So instead of using the 'predict()' result, always get the 'predict_proba()'!

However here, it must be taken into account that the majority of your users are not scientists and therefore have a biased representation of probabilities, with a tendency to overestimate low probability events and underestimate high probability events.

Figure from : Khaw et al. 2021 https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008871

Thus, to simplify this notion of probability, they can be expressed not as a percentage, but in explicit terms. The reliability of the AI prediction or decision will can be "absolutely certain", "certain", "probable" or "very uncertain".

Some models (live SVM) can give you poor estimates of the probabilities and therefore make the interpretation of the probabilities unreliable.

We recommend calibrating your model or at least, check their reliability with calibration curves.

## 09 APPENDICES

### APPENDIX 1: GLOSSARY

· Accountability: Accountability can be broken down into two subcomponents: answerability and auditability. Answerability refers to establishing a continuous chain of human responsibility across the whole AI project delivery workflow and demands that explanations and justifications of both the content of algorithmically supported decisions and the processes behind their production be offered by competent human authorities in plain, understandable, and coherent language. Auditability answers the question of how the designers and implementers of AI systems are to be held accountable. This aspect of accountability has to do with demonstrating both the responsibility of design and use practices and the justifiability of outcomes.

· Algorithm: An algorithm is a procedure or series of steps that provide instructions on how to take a series of inputs and produce an output. For instance, a recipe can be thought of as an algorithm that provides instructions for taking a series of inputs (i.e. the ingredients) and creating an output (e.g. a cake). In the case of machine learning, the algorithm is typically a series of instructions that instruct a software package to take a dataset (i.e. the input) and learn a model or discover some underlying pattern (i.e. the output).

· Algorithmic Audits: There are a variety of approaches to algorithmic auditing, which range from the targeted assessment of a system according to some metric (e.g. level of bias) to a broader approach that focuses on whether the system complies with a set of norms or regulatory area. While typically performed by professionals for the purpose of independent assessment, algorithmic audits have also been used by journalists, academics, and activists as a means of securing greater levels of transparency and accountability.

· Automated decision: An automated decision is the selection of an action or a recommendation made using computational processes. Automated decisions describe those that either augment or replace decisional work typically performed by humans alone. Most commonly, automated decisions are predictions about persons or conditions in the world derived from machine learning analysis of data about past events and its similarity to a given set of conditions.

· Automated decision system: An automated decision system (ADS) augments or replaces human decision-making by using computational processes to produce answers to questions either as discrete classifications (e.g. yes, no; male, female, non-binary; malignant, benign) or continuous scores (e.g. degree of creditworthiness, risk of crime occurrence, projected tumour growth). Most ADS produce predictions about persons or conditions using machine learning and other computational logic by calculating the probability that a given condition is met.

# 3- Interpretability

Machine Learning changed the way computer programs are done. Developers used to formalize a problem and code the rules that would transform input data into output data. Now, it is the model that determines the rules that link the input and output data through iterations and error minimization. It is this ability that gives all its power to Machine Learning and allows us to solve problems that exceed human formalization capabilities. But it is also coupled with a constraint: the rules applied by the model after training to make its predictions and decision may evade human control. For certain types of models, these rules sometimes remain unknown, even if interpretability techniques have made great progress in recent years. This is the famous "black box effect". However, when we decide to use Al to make decisions or make predictions that will have an impact on the lives of citizens, it is crucial, and soon to be regulatory, to keep control of the models and guarantee their explicability.

The interpretability of AI models is therefore becoming a major challenge, both for those who design them and for those who use them. It is a question of knowing which factors influence each decision and prediction (local interpretability) but also which rules govern the model in general (global interpretability).

Interpretability can be defined as having access to the features or variables that are driving the decisions or predictions of a model.

An Interpretable system becomes:

· Explicable: we can provide information and explanation (see the Explicability section)

· Transparent: it has a functioning intelligible to a human

· Provable: it can provide proof of the accuracy of the result

Whatever your use-case, it is critical to use interpretability methods.

If your system is critical, you should use directly interpretable models (regressions or simple decision trees), you can refer to Section 3.C.Direct Interpretability for more information.

If you are not required Direct Interpretability, are decided to use more complex models, you can use toolboxes to access indirect interpretability. You can refer to Section 3.D for more information, depending on the type of data (tabular, text or images).

# 4- Explicability

As described in introduction, AI is a system, with users to take into account and an interface to build. Once you have access to what factor influenced your prediction/decision, it comes the time to explain it to your users. That is what explicability is. Knowing your users, understanding not only their needs but their reluctances, choosing the right level of information, giving them control and ability to give feedbacks, all of these techniques will ensure more trust and adoption of your solution.

# A. UX studies

You need to know the appetite of users relative to AI to deliver the right level of explicability.

With explicability, we enter into UX Design and question the preference of users in terms of presentation of results. The level of explicability that accompanies the decision must correspond to the profile of the users. Depending on how AI will impact their work and life, but also on their maturity vis-à-vis this technology, not everyone will need the same granularity in the explanation.

To know the appetite of your users for AI, the best thing is to ask them the question through a short questionnaire. This will make it possible to detect the populations towards which it will be necessary to make a special effort to achieve genuine support.

Moreover, you won't give the same information to an expert or a novice. For example, for a medical diagnostic algorithm, you won't give the same information to doctors or patients. Doctors will need more technical information, patients more plain English ones. Workshops with your users and regular feedbacks are indispensable to fit your interface with their information requirements to trust your solution.

## A. For whom?

<!-- PageBreak -->

### A.1. The regulator

As mentioned in the section about legal risks in Introduction, the new European law on AI will describe different levels of criticality for AI models. Depending on the level, complete or partial interpretability will be asked by law and in addition to documentation, some audits might occur. Therefore, interpretability will become mandatory for many AI models.

### A.2. The developer or Data Scientist

The data scientist needs to access, as best as possible, the parameters of a model to understand it, to fix possible mistakes, to improve its performance and to stay in control.

#### A.3. The main user

The user needs information in order to best use the product or solution as well as to trust its recommendation. Adoption is driven by trust and very linked to the information that will be provided. We will get into more details about that in the Explicability section of these Guidelines.

#### A.4. The final user

The final user is the person who is the subject of the prediction or decision. That can be the same person as the main user or a different one. For example, we can have a skin diagnostic solution for doctors (main users) that concerns their patients (final users). This group of people may ask for information about the decision/prediction of the algorithm and in many case, they have the legal right to know what were the factor that lead to the decision/prediction.

# B. Of what?

We can be interested to have interpretability of the whole system or just of different parts of the system. We can look to understand a single prediction, all predictions, a part of the model, the whole model, the path that the data takes along the processing pipeline ...

## B.1. Global and Local

<!-- PageBreak -->

There are two main information that we want to access when we talk about Interpretability. We want to access what factors influenced each prediction and with what extend, that is called the Local Interpretability, and we also want to know what the factors of importance for the model are, that is the Global Interpretability.

In the case of simple algorithms like the regressions, the global interpretability is directly given by the coefficients of the model after training (remember to scale or normalize your data first, overwise you will not be able to interpret the results). With sklearn, just use 'model.coef_'. You can put them in a DataFrame with the variable names for simpler visualization :

pd. DataFrame ( {"Feature" : X_train . columns . tolist () , "Coefficients" : model . coef [0]})

In the case of more complex models, we will need to use additional tools to have access to an approximation of this information, like Lime or Shap or the Feature Importance function of sklearn. N.B. LIME and SHAP are local interpretability methods but they can still be used for the global interpretability.

You can refer to the sklearn MOOC part on feature importance here for more

information: Feature importance - Scikit-learn course

For the interpretability of the predictions (local), we see the same distinction between simple and more complex algorithms. With the simple models, we can directly apply the coefficients or the rules (for simple decision tree) to the data specific for each individual prediction. For more complex algorithms, we will again use additional tools (Lime, Shap ... ).

We will come back to the tools in more details in a dedicated section.

# C. Why not interpretable?

## C.1. The data complexity

There are different ways in which the data itself can make the system hard to interpret.

Some variables may contain information that is difficult to comprehend, for example medical or scientific information or expert technical measurements.

Moreover, during the Feature Engineering of the model construction, we may apply manipulations to the data that may lead to a loss of meaning. For example taking the log of a measure, using a dimension reduction method (i.e. PCA), combining variables ...

<!-- PageBreak -->

Finally, the storage of the data can add to the complexity if we lose the lineage and the contextual information that goes with it.

Le deep learning est une branche du ML qui se concentre sur l'entraînement de modèles comportant plusieurs couches de réseaux neuronaux artificiels, permettant au modèle d'extraire des motifs complexes dans les données d'entrée. Le deep learning a démontré des capacités remarquables dans différents domaines, notamment le traitement du langage naturel, la reconnaissance d'images et la synthèse vocale.

. Natural Language Processing (NLP): terme anglais signifiant le traitement du langage naturel. Il englobe les méthodes utilisées pour permettre aux ordinateurs de comprendre, analyser, manipuler et générer des séquences de mots en langage humain tel que l'anglais, le français, etc. Les applications courantes du NLP incluent la traduction automatique, la reconnaissance vocale ou encore le résumé de texte.

· Large Language Models (LLM) : terme anglais signifiant « grand modèle de langage », utilisé pour désigner un modèle de deep learning appliqué au domaine du natural language processing, et qui possède un grand nombre de paramètres. Les LLM ont démontré une capacité remarquable à générer du texte de manière cohérente, à répondre à des questions, à synthétiser des informations, mais aussi à produire du code dans des langages de programmation.

· IA Générative : terme faisant référence à la partie du machine learning qui se concentre sur les tâches génératives, c'est-à-dire la création de nouvelles

· Source : il s'agit de l'origine d'une information, généralement identifiée et datée. Les sources peuvent prendre différentes formes, telles que des études quantitatives statistiques, des transcriptions de discours publics, etc.

· Rapporteur : ce terme désigne l'entité qui communique une information. Cette information peut être relayée avec plus ou moins de fidélité. Un rapporteur peut être par exemple un professeur, un journal, ou même ChatGPT.

## Vers une première définition

Avant d'approfondir notre analyse de la qualité des informations obtenues par l'usage d'IA générative, il est essentiel de définir clairement ce que nous cherchons à évaluer. La notion de fiabilité de l'information peut sembler floue, et pourtant nous jugeons en continu la fiabilité des informations qui nous sont transmises.

Considérons un simple exemple : si quelqu'un prétend que la somme de 1 et 1 fait 3, alors nous mettrons naturellement en doute la sincérité du rapporteur ou l'adéquation entre sa compréhension des mathématiques et la nôtre. Notre évaluation de la fiabilité de l'information serait immédiate et intuitive. Étudions plus en détail le processus sous-jacent à ce jugement de fiabilité.

# Responsible AI: A competitive edge in the data and GenAI landscape

How Responsible Al enables the use of data, Al, and Gen Al technologies to create a strategic business advantage

<!-- PageBreak -->

<!-- PageHeader: Ekimetrics. -->

## Introduction

### Understand how and why AI makes a decision...

You have probably already applied for a loan from a bank. You have submitted your application for review by your account manager. Income, account management, personal situation, residual savings, downpayment: did you know that all these loan approval criteria are already analyzed by algorithms and artificial intelligence (AI)? Objective criteria? Are you sure?! How can you prove that you have not been discriminated against due to a black box effect? So what is a black box effect? It's a bit like trying to study a car engine without being able to open the hood. You input data into the box -the Al, a Machine Learning system for example- and results are output, which may be remarkable ... yet you're unable to explain the process that allowed the algorithm to make its choices. Understanding the reasons behind the decisions made by an algorithm is essential to ensure its accuracy and avoid bias (often the same discriminations as in the "real world", linked to gender, age, skin color or nationality1). In other words, the aim is to guarantee equal rights, whether for securing a loan, access to public services, hiring ...

### ... and make it strategic

And here's when we need to talk about responsible Al. Let's say that in our first example, you're no longer the one applying for the loan. You're the one who manages the bank or the IT system or the analytics. And for you, "Responsible AI" means "yet more new regulations, more rules to change and implement!". But if we tell you that responsible AI will help you optimize your costs, beef up your customer service or even your loyalty/satisfaction strategy, and easily maintain your platforms while complying with regulations, perhaps you'll see it as a major opportunity to build future-proof practices and business models. Let's rephrase: responsible AI does not have to be synonymous with constraints and compliance. On the contrary: because it is responsible, this approach to AI creates value and gives companies a true competitive edge.

Responsible AI is all the more critical now that generative AIs (see below) have entered with a bang into all strata of society. The biases remain the same as those of the "old" AI. But their effects have multiplied: using colossal volumes of data2 , these "GenAI" generate new data, which is in turn used as input for decision-making. How can we trust them, and guarantee that an organization's products and services are reliable? Responsible AI is therefore becoming a cornerstone of business strategy. And we're not talking here about 5, 10 or 15-year business strategies. We're talking about what can be implemented now, with today's know-how and knowledge. This white paper is a practical guide to responsible AI for business.

\* 1 There are already many examples of algorithmic discriminatory behaviors that led to scandals that have tarnished the reputation and business of large companies. Read: "Apple card investigated after gender discrimination complaints", "Amazon scraps secret Al recruiting tool that showed bias against women", "LAPD will end controversial program that aimed to predict where crimes would occur"

\* 2 Gartner predicts that, within three years, generative AI will produce 10% of all data, i.e. tens of billions of gigabytes. Read: https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2021-10-18-gartner-identifies-the-top-strategic-technology-trends-for-2022

<!-- PageFooter: page 02 -->
<!-- PageBreak -->

<!-- PageHeader: Ekimetrics. -->

## · Generative AI for dummies

### Generative AIs create content...

... as if they were you, based on one of your requests. Text, images, video, sound: they magnify human creative processes; it only takes them a few seconds to generate a text (with ChatGPT3) or an image (with Midjourney).

### What is the difference with the "old" AI?

Until now, AIs were based mainly on "structured" data: descriptive, numerical information in spreadsheets (business accounts, temperature measurements for weather forecasts, sales figures, etc.). Generative AIs are based on "unstructured" data (text, images, video, sound); in a way, they create "new" content.

### What challenges to achieve what success?

### Relevance.

How do we control hallucinations and biases while respecting the regulatory framework, in a context with a low acceptable error on decision-making? How do we ensure that the content is contextualized and actionable in a specific sector, business, use and time?

# B. Probabilities

By highlighting the relevant information, giving the user as much context as possible, it becomes possible to erase the feeling of no longer having any control over the decisions made by the machine.

The first information that will interest the user is to know how reliable the AI recommendation is. We too often set a default decision (i.e. threshold of 50% for a binary decision), and only give users the final decision: yes or no. Knowing the probability of a prediction can be a key acceptability factor. Indeed, depending on

<!-- PageBreak -->

whether this percentage is 60% or 90% for a binary classification, the confidence in your model's predictions will not be the same.

So instead of using the 'predict()' result, always get the 'predict_proba()'!

However here, it must be taken into account that the majority of your users are not scientists and therefore have a biased representation of probabilities, with a tendency to overestimate low probability events and underestimate high probability events.

Figure from : Khaw et al. 2021 https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008871

Thus, to simplify this notion of probability, they can be expressed not as a percentage, but in explicit terms. The reliability of the AI prediction or decision will can be "absolutely certain", "certain", "probable" or "very uncertain".

## B.1. Calibration

Some models (live SVM) can give you poor estimates of the probabilities and therefore make the interpretation of the probabilities unreliable.

We recommend calibrating your model or at least, check their reliability with calibration curves.

## A. For whom?

<!-- PageBreak -->

### A.1. The regulator

As mentioned in the section about legal risks in Introduction, the new European law on AI will describe different levels of criticality for AI models. Depending on the level, complete or partial interpretability will be asked by law and in addition to documentation, some audits might occur. Therefore, interpretability will become mandatory for many AI models.

### A.2. The developer or Data Scientist

The data scientist needs to access, as best as possible, the parameters of a model to understand it, to fix possible mistakes, to improve its performance and to stay in control.

#### A.3. The main user

The user needs information in order to best use the product or solution as well as to trust its recommendation. Adoption is driven by trust and very linked to the information that will be provided. We will get into more details about that in the Explicability section of these Guidelines.

#### A.4. The final user

The final user is the person who is the subject of the prediction or decision. That can be the same person as the main user or a different one. For example, we can have a skin diagnostic solution for doctors (main users) that concerns their patients (final users). This group of people may ask for information about the decision/prediction of the algorithm and in many case, they have the legal right to know what were the factor that lead to the decision/prediction.

# B. Of what?

We can be interested to have interpretability of the whole system or just of different parts of the system. We can look to understand a single prediction, all predictions, a part of the model, the whole model, the path that the data takes along the processing pipeline ...

## B.1. Global and Local

<!-- PageBreak -->

There are two main information that we want to access when we talk about Interpretability. We want to access what factors influenced each prediction and with what extend, that is called the Local Interpretability, and we also want to know what the factors of importance for the model are, that is the Global Interpretability.

In the case of simple algorithms like the regressions, the global interpretability is directly given by the coefficients of the model after training (remember to scale or normalize your data first, overwise you will not be able to interpret the results). With sklearn, just use 'model.coef_'. You can put them in a DataFrame with the variable names for simpler visualization :

pd. DataFrame ( {"Feature" : X_train . columns . tolist () , "Coefficients" : model . coef [0]})

In the case of more complex models, we will need to use additional tools to have access to an approximation of this information, like Lime or Shap or the Feature Importance function of sklearn. N.B. LIME and SHAP are local interpretability methods but they can still be used for the global interpretability.

You can refer to the sklearn MOOC part on feature importance here for more

information: Feature importance - Scikit-learn course

For the interpretability of the predictions (local), we see the same distinction between simple and more complex algorithms. With the simple models, we can directly apply the coefficients or the rules (for simple decision tree) to the data specific for each individual prediction. For more complex algorithms, we will again use additional tools (Lime, Shap ... ).

We will come back to the tools in more details in a dedicated section.

# C. Why not interpretable?

## C.1. The data complexity

There are different ways in which the data itself can make the system hard to interpret.

Some variables may contain information that is difficult to comprehend, for example medical or scientific information or expert technical measurements.

Moreover, during the Feature Engineering of the model construction, we may apply manipulations to the data that may lead to a loss of meaning. For example taking the log of a measure, using a dimension reduction method (i.e. PCA), combining variables ...

<!-- PageBreak -->

Finally, the storage of the data can add to the complexity if we lose the lineage and the contextual information that goes with it.

## 3· Interpretability pillar

### Core concept

Ensure access to the factors (characteristics and/or variables) that determine a model's decisions and/or predictions

### What are the risks?

· For your business customers > inability to explain model decisions/predictions. Example: what factors enable an algorithm to establish a medical diagnosis? Or refuse a loan?

· For your end customers > discrimination, prejudice against the legal right to know the factors leading to the decision/prediction (black box effect).

· For your organization > loss of control over your model (black box effect), legal and compliance risks, business risks

Where do you start? For directly interpretable algorithms:

V Use simple regressions and decision trees

For algorithms that are not directly interpretable:

V Add control libraries or algorithmic layers to determine how the model works (Lime and Shape are frequently used tools)

What's the competitive advantage?

· For your customers > trust

· For your organization > control your system, compliance, rigorous customer service (= giving objective reasons to end customers)

## WHAT IS A "BLACK BOX EFFECT"?

It's the inability to explain how an algorithmic model makes its decisions. In other words, it's providing the link between the initial data and the final decision.

## DIRECTLY, NOT DIRECTLY INTERPRETABLE: WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE?

There are 3 types of directly interpretable algorithm: linear regression, logistic regression and the simple decision tree. This type of algorithm provides direct access to a model's characteristics.

Other algorithms are not directly interpretable: this is the case for most of the models used: set models, SVMs, artificial neural networks, etc. In these cases, additional toolboxes are needed to access the interpretability of the model and prediction.

. Approach: We developed and implemented state-of-the-art interpretability methods to break down the different effects using an Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM).

# 4- Explicability

As described in introduction, AI is a system, with users to take into account and an interface to build. Once you have access to what factor influenced your prediction/decision, it comes the time to explain it to your users. That is what explicability is. Knowing your users, understanding not only their needs but their reluctances, choosing the right level of information, giving them control and ability to give feedbacks, all of these techniques will ensure more trust and adoption of your solution.

# A. UX studies

You need to know the appetite of users relative to AI to deliver the right level of explicability.

With explicability, we enter into UX Design and question the preference of users in terms of presentation of results. The level of explicability that accompanies the decision must correspond to the profile of the users. Depending on how AI will impact their work and life, but also on their maturity vis-à-vis this technology, not everyone will need the same granularity in the explanation.

To know the appetite of your users for AI, the best thing is to ask them the question through a short questionnaire. This will make it possible to detect the populations towards which it will be necessary to make a special effort to achieve genuine support.

Moreover, you won't give the same information to an expert or a novice. For example, for a medical diagnostic algorithm, you won't give the same information to doctors or patients. Doctors will need more technical information, patients more plain English ones. Workshops with your users and regular feedbacks are indispensable to fit your interface with their information requirements to trust your solution.

context_data.content:
# 3- Interpretability

Machine Learning changed the way computer programs are done. Developers used to formalize a problem and code the rules that would transform input data into output data. Now, it is the model that determines the rules that link the input and output data through iterations and error minimization. It is this ability that gives all its power to Machine Learning and allows us to solve problems that exceed human formalization capabilities. But it is also coupled with a constraint: the rules applied by the model after training to make its predictions and decision may evade human control. For certain types of models, these rules sometimes remain unknown, even if interpretability techniques have made great progress in recent years. This is the famous "black box effect". However, when we decide to use Al to make decisions or make predictions that will have an impact on the lives of citizens, it is crucial, and soon to be regulatory, to keep control of the models and guarantee their explicability.

The interpretability of AI models is therefore becoming a major challenge, both for those who design them and for those who use them. It is a question of knowing which factors influence each decision and prediction (local interpretability) but also which rules govern the model in general (global interpretability).

Interpretability can be defined as having access to the features or variables that are driving the decisions or predictions of a model.

An Interpretable system becomes:

· Explicable: we can provide information and explanation (see the Explicability section)

· Transparent: it has a functioning intelligible to a human

· Provable: it can provide proof of the accuracy of the result

Whatever your use-case, it is critical to use interpretability methods.

If your system is critical, you should use directly interpretable models (regressions or simple decision trees), you can refer to Section 3.C.Direct Interpretability for more information.

If you are not required Direct Interpretability, are decided to use more complex models, you can use toolboxes to access indirect interpretability. You can refer to Section 3.D for more information, depending on the type of data (tabular, text or images).

context_data.content:
#### 3.1.3.A. The black box problem

Opacity surrounding the technical, internal decision- making processes of generative Al models is popularly known as the "black box problem."277 Generative Al models, most ubiquitously built on deep neural networks with hundreds of billions of internal connections,278 have become so complex that their internal decision-making processes are no longer traceable or interpretable to even the most advanced expert observers. This means that, while the inputs and outputs of a system can be observed, developers cannot explain in detail why specific inputs correspond to specific outputs.279

Increasing interpretability (i.e., the comprehension of how an Al model generates a specific output) is crucial. For developers and model trainers, understanding how models make decisions allows them to identify and correct biases, errors, and unintended behaviors, leading to more robust and efficient systems. This ability to anticipate and mitigate errors ensures that Al outputs are accurate and ethically sound. For lay people who use Al models, interpretability empowers them to make informed decisions and detect when the Al might be malfunctioning or producing biased outputs, enabling timely corrective actions. This reduces the risk of relying on faulty Al recommendations and fosters confidence in using these technologies. For individuals impacted by Al decisions, such as in healthcare, education, and finance, interpretability ensures that they can understand and challenge incorrect outcomes. Overall, increasing

interpretability helps prevent and mitigate unforeseen negative consequences, making Al systems more transparent, reliable, and aligned with societal values.

In the future, Al models may become less opaque. The field of explainable AI (XAI) seeks to develop new techniques and methods to improve the ability of users to comprehend the inner workings of Al models. 280 For instance, Anthropic has achieved a breakthrough to enhance the interpretability of language models.281 Instead of focusing on individual neurons, researchers at Anthropic analyze groups of neurons as features, revealing clearer patterns. Recently, Anthropic's researchers managed to extract millions of features from one of their Al models, creating a rough conceptual map of the model's internal states. 282 This approach may improve transparency and control over Al behavior.

Naturally, the interfaces of the tools made available to users play a crucial role in an Al model's potential for misuse. When providers offer their models through web-based chatbots, such as ChatGPT, they maintain significant control over how the tool is used.832 Conversely, API interfaces, which necessitate more technical knowledge from users, offer significantly greater flexibility and, consequently, a higher potential for misuse. In any case, it is primarily through the design of their systems that Al companies can limit the risks.

<!-- PageHeader: CHAPTER 5 Regulatory initiatives REGULATING UNDER UNCERTAINTY: Governance Options for Generative AI -->

Interestingly, the revised PLD provides in Recital 30 that "the assessment of defectiveness should involve an objective analysis of the safety that the public at large is entitled to expect, and not refer to the safety that any particular person is entitled to expect". However, does the public have sufficient awareness of the recognized risk of hallucinations inherent in models like ChatGPT, especially when it has been explicitly stated that these models can make errors? Recital 31 specifies that "warnings or other information provided with a product cannot be considered sufficient to make an otherwise defective product safe, since defectiveness should be determined by reference to the safety that the public at large is entitled to expect." Thus, one could conclude that merely warning users that a model might hallucinate, produce inaccurate information, or behave unpredictably does not suffice to exempt that product from being deemed defective. On the other hand, would it be reasonable to consider that the public expects that such models never produce inaccurate or illegal content? For the moment, there do not seem to be any clear, definitive answers to these questions.

Moreover, it is worth mentioning that "the reasonably foreseeable use of the product"1289 should be considered in the assessment. Does this suggest that the providers of generative AI chatbots should foresee that students, journalists, or lawyers will use their tool and rely on the information it generates? While the answer to that question is uncertain, it is evident that providers of AI systems must foresee potential misuse. Recital 31 provides that the determination "of reasonably foreseeable use should also encompass misuse that is not unreasonable under the circumstances, such as the foreseeable behaviour of a user of machinery resulting from a lack of concentration or the foreseeable behaviour

of certain user groups such as children." Consequently, providers should expect that schoolchildren might use their tools for doing their homework or that teenagers might seek to create deepfakes.

The revised Product Liability Directive also mentions "the effect on the product of its ability to continue to learn or acquire new features after it is placed on the market or put into service."1290 An Al system could be deemed defective due to knowledge acquired after its release. Recital 32 states that "a manufacturer that designs a product with the ability to develop unexpected behaviour should remain liable for behaviour that causes harm."

Once again, it is challenging to ascertain the full impact of such a provision at this stage. The text appears to hold developers of advanced AI models liable for the most unpredictable effects of their applications. In a context where it is inherently impossible to fully anticipate the behavior of machine-learning tools, this responsibility could be substantial.

### d) Possible claimants and repairable damage

While the proposal substantially raises the number of potential defendants, it is relatively narrow in defining who can sue and what kind of compensation they can pursue. Only natural persons are entitled to compensation.1291 This implies that legal entities, beginning with businesses, are not entitled to initiate legal proceedings based on product liability against a provider of an AI system.

The revised PLD extends the scope of recoverable damages to cover death, physical injury, or property damage (unless the property is used for professional

\* 1289 New Product Liability Directive, art. 7(2)(b).

\* 1290 Id. art. 7(2)(c). 1291 Id. art. 5.

purposes), as well as losses resulting from "medically recognized damage to psychological health"1292 or "destruction or corruption of data that are not used for professional purposes."1293

## 1.16. Probability calibration

# C. Confidence intervals

Another interesting information to provide to the users: the confidence interval. This allows you to know on which subcategories of data the model is reliable, and for which, not so much. It is directly related to the variability in the prediction for a certain range of predictions and very much depends on how much data of each subcategories the model has been trained. For example, if a model has been trained with a lot of Caucasian faces and a few Asian ones, it will tend to be more reliable for the first class.

<!-- PageBreak -->

## C.1. Cross validation

You can get a first measure of the variability of your overall model performance by doing cross-validation (3.1. Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance ), but it is not enough as it doesn't go into the details of performance for the subcategories.

## C.2. Mapie

You can use a toolbox called Mapie (MAPIE - Model Agnostic Prediction Interval Estimator - MAPIE 0.6.5 documentation ) which is a model agnostic solution that works for both regression and classification problems.

Source : Taquet et al. 2022 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12274.pdf

You can find a video explaining the solution here : https://crossminds.ai/video/mapie- model-agnostic-prediction-interval-estimator-614bc17e3c7a224a9090211b/

And articles here:

· With MAPIE, uncertainties are back in machine learning !

· https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.12274.pdf

# D. Human agency/control

In a Pew Research report from 2018 on AI and the Future of Humans (Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Humans ) concern about Human agency came out as the main concern. They talk about the fear that : 'the use of Al reduces individuals' control over their lives'.

And the European Commission High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence (AI HLEG 2018 : Requirements of Trustworthy Al ) defines 'human agency and oversight' as the first of seven key elements in their "Trustworthy Al" framework. They state that 'Al systems should support human autonomy and decision-making, as prescribed by the principle of respect for human autonomy. This requires that AI systems should both act as enablers to a democratic, flourishing and equitable society by supporting the user's agency and foster fundamental rights, and allow for human oversight."

Following these reports, it is fundamental that your systems always keep the 'humans in the loop' and should never be fully autonomous. A human should always make the final decision.

<!-- PageBreak -->

This recommendation goes hand-in-hand with explicability as you should give all the necessary information to the users to make the decision.

And the design of the interface of the product or solution you are developing will be key here.

# E. Feedback loops

Because keeping people in the loop is fundamental as we have just seen, care will be taken to encourage user feedback on the solution.

## E.1. Report a mistake

If your user considers that the system has made a mistake in the prediction or decision, they must be able to express it. You should include, in the design of your solution, a way for them to do so.

This will increase the trust of your users for your solution greatly.

## E.2. Performance in production

In addition, this feedback can be used to measure the performance in production, detect drifts and give a database to eventually retrain your model.

Moreover, you can also detect bugs in the system and be able to strengthen its robustness and performance.

And here is an interesting article on the feedback loop topic: Feedback Loops-Friend or Foe?

<!-- PageBreak -->

Despite these techniques, the problem of confabulations is not easy to solve. A recent study by Nezhurina et al. revealed significant deficiencies in the reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), which were trained at the largest available scales and claimed to possess strong functional abilities.275 When presented with a simple, concise common- sense problem, easily solvable by humans, these models frequently failed to provide correct solutions. Furthermore, they exhibited strong overconfidence in their incorrect answers and often generated nonsensical, confabulation-like explanations to justify their flawed responses, making them appear plausible. Standard interventions, such as enhanced prompting or multistep re-evaluation, were ineffective in correcting these errors. The study calls for an urgent reassessment of the purported capabilities of current LLMs and the development of standardized benchmarks to identify basic reasoning deficits that existing evaluation procedures and benchmarks may overlook.276

#### 3.1.3. Opacity

Each of the risks detailed above is troubling, but they may be even more concerning because of the lack of transpa- rency into how generative Al models and their developers operate. This "lack of transparency"-or "opacity"-has two primary causes: the technical difficulties of understanding exactly how generative Al models produce their outputs, and a lack of transparency by leading model providers into their internal development and governance processes.

# D. Toolboxes for indirect interpretability

There are many tools to 'open the black box' and get information about the model, but keep in mind that there are all indirect variable estimations and are just indications and certainly not exact information.

Most of these techniques are universal (model agnostic) and can be applied to all algorithms/models. However, certain tools are better suited for certain types of data and certain type of models. We will mainly focus on two toolboxes: Lime and SHAP as there are the ones most widely used.

## D.1. Structured data

For structured data, and for models that are not directly interpretable, we suggest the use of these two toolboxes, LIME and Shap.

## D.1.a. LIME

The acronym LIME stands for Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations. It provides local interpretability for your classifications and can be applied to any model. It is based on this paper : https://arxiv.org/pdf/1602.04938.pdf and you can also watch this video for a high-level explanation : KDD2016 paper 573

LIME uses a local surrogate model trained on perturbations of the data point we are investigating for explanations.

Source : https://github.com/marcotcr/lime

Even though we can use any interpretable model as the local surrogate, the paper uses a Lasso regression to induce sparsity in explanations.

The advantages of the technique are:

· Both the methodology and the explanations are very intuitive to explain to a human being.

· It is Model-agnostic.

. It works for structured as well as unstructured data (more on that later).

· Available in R and Python (original implementation by the authors of the paper).

<!-- PageBreak -->

meta.doc_name: Ada (technique)_Standards - Interpretability

context_data.content:
## D.1.c. Other methods

They are many other interpretability methods, we will not get into the details, we will refer you to this online book by Christoph Molnar: Interpretable Machine Learning

We will still list them here to be exhaustive.

### Global Model-Agnostic Methods:

· The partial dependence plot is a feature effect method.

· Accumulated local effect plots is another feature effect method that works when features are dependent.

<!-- PageBreak -->

· Feature interaction (H-statistic) quantifies to what extent the prediction is the result of joint effects of the features.

· Functional decomposition is a central idea of interpretability and a technique that decomposes the complex prediction function into smaller parts.

· Permutation feature importance measures the importance of a feature as an increase in loss when the feature is permuted.

· Global surrogate models replaces the original model with a directly interpretable model for interpretation.

· Prototypes and criticisms are representative data point of a distribution and can be used to enhance interpretability.

Local Model-Agnostic Methods:

· Individual conditional expectation curves are the building blocks for partial dependence plots and describe how changing a feature changes the prediction.

· Scoped rules (anchors) are rules that describe which feature values anchor a prediction, in the sense that they lock the prediction in place.

· Counterfactual explanations explain a prediction by examining which features would need to be changed to achieve a desired prediction.

· Shapley values are an attribution method that fairly assigns the prediction to individual features.

### And of course:

· Local surrogate models (LIME) explain a prediction by replacing the complex model with a locally interpretable surrogate model.

· SHAP is another computation method for Shapley values, but also proposes global interpretation methods based on combinations of Shapley values across the data.

If you don't want to read a whole book, here are two papers reviewing the subject:

· PNAS

· NCBI - WWW Error Blocked Diagnostic

#### D.2. Text

We have seen the different toolboxes and methods for tabular, structured data, but how can you do for text? It can be very important to know what words have been critical in order to: assign a sentiment to the sentence, categorize a text or whatever your NLP task was.

LIME and SHAP propose solutions specific to NLP. We will look into them and add another option too.

## D.2.a. LIME

<!-- PageBreak -->

lime

The same way that LIME has a tabular explainer, it also has a text explainer ( package - lime 0.1 documentation ).

You initiate the explainer, after having trained a model for sentient analysis for example:

class_names=['negative', 'positive'] explainer = LimeTextExplainer(class_names=class_names)

And you get the explainer to explain an instance ('text'):

exp = explainer. explain_instance(text, model. predict_proba, num_features=6) And you get that illustration:

It gives you the usual LIME plot with the prediction probabilities of the model for this prediction (on the left) and what were the features (here words) important for the prediction.

This important addition is the highlighted text at the bottom of the figure, that shows you the words, in the sentence, that were important, color coded as a function of the possible labels (here blue for positive, orange for negative sentiment).

As for tabular data, LIME is easy to use and relatively fast.

## D.2.b. SHAP

The process with SHAP is very similar, there are just more visualization options. You

can access the documentation here : Text examples - SHAP latest documentation , from which we took the following examples.

You start with the explainer on your pretrained model: explainer = shap. Explainer (pred)

You compute the shap values for a specific instance: shap_values = explainer (data [ ' text ' ] [ : 0] )

And you visualize the result: shap. plots. text (shap_values)

<!-- PageBreak -->
